item.title: Singapore Boffins Weave a GUI Into Fabric
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Researchers at the National University of Singapore have developed a machine-washable electronic fabric that can turn clothing into an interactive graphical user interface. The prototype reportedly survived 50 gentle machine washes and 1,000 bending cycles, though it still relies on external batteries and controllers. The Register reports: The development could lead - at some point - to a "future in which clothing functions as a pervasive, multimodal human-computer interface," according to the study published in peer-reviewed science journal Nature this week. The paper shows someone interacting with computing devices using the sleeve of a wool sweater (no jokes about the Windows ugly sweater please, this is serious). The researchers, led by Singapore National University research engineer Fu Heng, claim this is a big leap forward.
"This fiber-centric approach shifts wearable electronics from flexible panels toward truly textile-native architectures, laying the groundwork for fabrics that visualize, sense, communicate and compute as naturally as the garments they inhabit," the paper says. The researchers claim to have developed a scalable process to make millimeter-thick fibers. Using lasers to strip the insulation from specific spots on the thin copper wires, they attached light-emitting chips to the exposed sections, creating electrical connections to the chips. Thousands of chips were connected to the wires with extreme precision using this process.
The fibers were then fed into a transparent plastic tube, and made pressure-sensitive by adding two strips of a compressible, conductive polymer into a second longitudinal channel in the tube. The paper says they could make fibers 10 meters long using this method, and that they are thin and flexible enough to be woven into or attached to fabrics. The researchers were also able to add "peripherals" such as a microphone, a speaker, a temperature sensor and a light sensor.

item.title: Your Client Is Borrowing From You: The Cash Exposure Math of a Freelance Project
item.author: azizfromgroundwork
item.content:encoded: Most freelancers think about payment terms as a question of trust. Will this client pay? Do I seem difficult if I ask for a deposit?There is a more useful way to look at it. Every hour you work before you are paid for it is money you have lent to your client, interest-free, with no security. The amount you are owed at any moment is your : the value of work you have delivered minus the cash you have received. It rises as you work, falls when a payment lands, and it is exactly what you lose if the client disappears tomorrow.Payment terms decide how big that number gets and how long it stays there. The difference between a good structure and a bad one is not a few percent. On the same project, it is four times as much money at risk.Take one project and run it three ways.A $12,000 build, ten weeks long, with the work spread evenly: $1,200 of work delivered each week. Exposure at the end of any week is:exposure = work delivered so far - cash received so far A negative number means the client has paid ahead of the work. A positive number is your loan to them.The most common default. You invoice $12,000 when the project ends at week 10, and the client pays 30 days later, around the end of week 14.Peak exposure: $12,000, held for four weeks. For fourteen weeks, you have been financing the client's project, and for the last four the entire fee is outstanding. If they go quiet in week 12, you have lost three months of work, not one invoice.The usual "fair" split. $6,000 arrives before you start; the other $6,000 is invoiced at week 10, net 30. Half of Structure A, which is why the deposit feels like the fix. But notice the shape: for the first five weeks the client is carrying the risk, and for the last nine it is all on you. The deposit protects the start of the project, and the start is the part that rarely goes wrong.Structure C: Four MilestonesSame $12,000, split into four payments of $3,000: a deposit before work starts, then one payment at the end of week 4, one at the end of week 7, and the last at handover in week 10. Milestone invoices are due in 7 days, the final one in 14.Peak exposure: $3,000, and the project is fully paid two weeks earlier. Same client, same work, same total fee. A quarter of the risk of Structure A.Put the three side by side, and a pattern falls out:peak exposure ≈ the largest payment you are waiting for In Structure A, the only payment is $12,000, so that is what you can lose. In Structure C, no single payment is bigger than $3,000, so no moment in the project has more than about $3,000 at stake.You can design for this directly. Decide the most you are willing to lose if a client vanishes, then size the payments so none of them is bigger than that. If your answer is $3,000 and the project is $12,000, you need at least four payments. The negotiation stops being about trust and becomes arithmetic.Late Payment Is Worse Than a Low RateExposure has two dimensions: how much, and for how long. Freelancers negotiate hard on the first and accept whatever they get on the second.Suppose the Structure A client pays 30 days late, in week 18 instead of week 14. Your $12,000 of exposure now lasts eight weeks after handover instead of four. If you would otherwise cover your own bills on a credit card at, say, 24% a year, carrying $12,000 for an extra four weeks costs about $220:$12,000 × 24% × 4/52 ≈ $222 That is roughly the cost of knocking 2% off your fee, except nobody asked you to agree to it.Now, run the same 30-day delay on Structure C. The late payment is the final $3,000, so the cost is about $55. Milestones do not just cap the risk; they shrink the damage of the most common thing that goes wrong.What Makes a Milestone Actually WorkSplitting the invoice is the easy part. Three details decide whether the structure holds when a project goes sideways.Tie each payment to something the client can see. "Phase 2 complete" invites an argument about what complete means. "Staging site live with checkout working" does not. A milestone the client can verify by clicking a link is a milestone they cannot dispute.Do not start the next phase until the last payment lands. This is the clause that turns a schedule into protection. Without it, a client who is two weeks late on milestone 2 is also two weeks into milestone 3, and your exposure is quietly back to Structure A levels. Put it in the contract in one sentence so pausing work is following the agreement, not making a threat.Shorten the terms on everything but the last invoice. Net 30 on a milestone mid-project means you keep working while you wait, which adds a full phase of unpaid work to your exposure. Seven days on milestones is normal and rarely questioned.Before you send your next proposal, take five minutes:Write down the project fee and how many weeks it will take.Divide the fee by the weeks to get your weekly work value.Sketch when each payment would actually arrive, terms included.Find the week where work delivered minus cash received is highest.Ask yourself whether you could lose that number and still pay your rent.If the answer is no, the fix is not a better client. It is a different payment structure, and it costs nothing to propose.AI disclosure: this article was written with the help of AI.

item.title: Can You Build an Agent Entirely in SQL? Almost
item.author: Nicholas Lisac
item.content:encoded: When you think of an agent, you think of the LLM - the back-and-forth with the model - but for it to be an agent, it has to . It has to have what is called a 'ReAct loop' in which the agent itself interacts with its environment, calls tools, and decides when its turn is done.That seems very complicated - you have to create the conditions for the loop, you have to provide tools, you have to interpret the responses and route the messages with logic.In addition to the ReAct loop, you need other things. You need chat history, the live working transcript, sessions, tool definitions, an environment in which to execute code, a way to compact the conversation, a place to store retrieved information. I wanted to see if I could build all of this in SQL. And I basically did. Its name is Tables.Tables is tables. Tables runs in a web app, but they don't have to. When you export from the web app, you get a single .sqlite file - a cartridge - and inside that file is the Python code that boots it: python3 your-agent.sqlite3 "What tables do I have?" and they talk back to you.Tables is built on SQLite. SQLite does need a small amount of external piping to come to life - in my case a bit of JavaScript for the web app, or a little Python for the CLI. To be honest about what "almost" means: what lives outside the file is one HTTPS call out to a model, the ferry that carries it, the thing that draws the results on screen, and your API keys. The agent's entire state and control flow are the file. Everything else is the HTTPS transportation layer.The loop is just a trigger.The core loop is a trigger. When a new row is written to the `messages` table, the trigger fires and the cascade starts: it hands the active context to the model, writes the model's answer back into `messages` as a new row, and that insert fires the same trigger again.If the answer contained a tool call, a second trigger runs the tool and its result lands in `messages` too, which continues the cascade. It repeats until the model stops asking for tools. That's the whole loop, and it needs one flag to exist at all: SQLite doesn't fire triggers from inside triggers by default, so the file sets `PRAGMA recursive_triggers = ON` and calls itself to life.The model's main tool is `execute_sql` - it thinks and acts inside a SQLite database, which is its whole environment. I did build out the rest of the tool set because I wanted something I could actually use: `search_web` and `fetch_url` because those are table stakes, `materialize` to turn raw JSON from a tool result into a real table with `json_each()` so the data doesn't have to be retyped through the model, and `search_documents` / `ingest_document` backed by an FTS5 table for recall.Messages are a table. Sessions are a table. The list of tools - a table. Approval rules? Table. The active context is a view that handles compaction. And as mentioned before, the loop is a trigger.There are some cool things that fall out of this when compared to other agent harnesses. Tables is literally one file. You can take your .sqlite3, send it to another computer, open tables.nicholaslisac.com, load the cartridge, and your agent is good to go - same conversation, same data, same identity - or run the Python that's sitting in the file and never open a browser. The API key never travels in the file; it gets paired once per machine for security.The chat history is native and easily explorable. Everything the agent has ever done or seen is in the SQLite database it operates from, and nothing is more than a SQL query away. Every write is journaled with who made it - the agent, you at the keyboard, or the interface on your behalf - so a turn can be undone without undoing your own work.Everything the agent learns ends up in the same place as everything you give it. Drop a CSV on the window, and it becomes a typed table; have it fetch a page and materialize the results, and that becomes a table too. After that they all swim the same way, because for the agent there is no difference between its own history and your data - it's all just rows and columns.Tables is naturally sandboxed to their database file, with the exception of their web capabilities. The agent can't touch your filesystem, can't install anything, can't notify you. It can't even break its own harness - the internal tables are protected from DDL and DML, on the agent's path and yours.You also get a scratchpad so Tables acts as your own SQL workbench: runs your query and shares the result with the agent, runs it privately and the agent never sees it. And if you pin a query you like, it becomes an artifact.Is this the future of Agent harnesses?!Absolutely not. I wondered if I could build an AI agent loop with SQL as the engine and set out to see if it worked. I got a little carried away and made an entire web app to prove a point. It's part research project, part portfolio piece. And I like it.Tables is not a coding agent. It doesn't have access to other files on your computer. It can't do most things people want out of their AI in 2026. Tables is just tables. But those tables can talk back to you, do real work in a database, do analysis and gather information from around the internet, and prove that SQL is (almost) as powerful as languages like Python or TypeScript.The code is open - you can see it on GitHub, and you can check out the explainer here or go right to the app here: tables.nicholaslisac.com. You can use Tables, but you will need to BYOK, whether that is local or cloud.No guarantee of performance or success - but it will probably be fun to talk to Tables.

item.title: People Are Vibe Coding Their Way to Better TVs
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Frustrated by intrusive ads, sluggish interfaces, and data tracking, smart TV owners are using AI coding tools and open-source projects to strip unwanted software from their televisions and build customized home screens. The Verge reports: Several vibe-coded TV-debloating projects exploded in popularity over the weekend. Cleanyourtv (known as tv-vibehack until the 19th), tv-detox, and dumbtv all claim to accomplish similar things -- remove sponsored ads, debloat the TV so it runs faster, and block unwanted data collection that tracks what you're watching -- without hacking, or rooting, the TV. By default, they all also replace the TV's built-in app launcher with simpler ones. Many users are going a step further and vibe-coding their own replacement launchers, like the Pokemon one below.
Most of the projects we've seen so far focus on TVs that run on Android and Google TV operating systems (such as TCL, Hisense, Sony, and older Amazon Fire products), using existing developer modes and the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) to tweak settings and apply (and remove) packages. According to the GitHub pages, they can also work with some Fire TV products that use a custom fork of Android (although likely not on the new Vega-based Fire TV Sticks). Because they use built-in developer tools, they don't require root access or firmware hacking, and they're reversible. Even projects that totally change the look of the interface just use Android's ability to install custom launchers -- in many cases with an assist from Claude Code or a similar tool to create the new launcher, too.

item.title: Five SEO “Errors” on My Static Site That Weren’t Errors
item.author: Alex
item.content:encoded: I run a small bilingual tutoring site, Intellix Tutoring. It is static HTML built with Jekyll on GitHub Pages: 68 pages, half in English and half in Italian, on a domain registered at the end of May.This week, I went through Google Search Console and a third-party SEO audit, which between them reported dozens of problems. Almost none of them needed fixing. One "fix" would have made things worse, and the only real issue took a one-line regex.Here are the five, and how I checked each one.1. "Page with redirect: Validation failed"Search Console listed four URLs under "Page with redirect", and the validation I had started in September said :http://www.intellixtutoring.com/ http://intellixtutoring.com/ https://www.intellixtutoring.com/ https://intellixtutoring.com/it First check: does each one go straight to the final URL?for u in http://www.intellixtutoring.com/ http://intellixtutoring.com/ \ https://www.intellixtutoring.com/ https://intellixtutoring.com/it; do echo "== $u" curl -sIL "$u" | grep -iE '^(HTTP/|location:)' done Each returned a single 301 to the canonical address (HTTPS, no www, trailing slash) and then a 200. That is exactly what you want.The validation fails because "Validate fix" asks Google to confirm that these URLs no longer redirect. They are supposed to redirect, so it will fail every time. This report is a list of URLs Google won't index because they point somewhere else, not a to-do list.2. "Discovered – currently not indexed" (39 pages)This one looked serious: 39 of 68 pages known to Google but never fetched. Before blaming Google, I crawled the site myself with a Googlebot user agent, starting from the home page and the sitemap:all 68 sitemap URLs return 200no in meta tags or headersevery page has a self-referencing canonicalevery sitemap URL is linked from at least three other pages, and the deepest is four clicks from the home pageno internal link points at a redirect or a 404Nothing technical was blocking those pages. The domain is about four months old and has very few links from other sites, so Google crawls it slowly. "Discovered" means the URL is in Google's queue and hasn't been worth a fetch yet.The crawl did find one thing worth changing: the home page linked to none of the 26 blog posts. They were reachable only through the blog index. That is a signal problem, not an indexing bug, and it's the kind of thing a crawl shows you and a dashboard doesn't.What actually helps here: request indexing by hand for the most important URLs (Search Console gives you a small daily quota), link important pages from the pages Google already visits, and earn links from other sites.3. Rich Results: "Invalid datetime value"Google's Rich Results Test passed every post: valid Article, Breadcrumb, and Organization items, no errors. It did flag four optional warnings on the article markup:Invalid datetime value for "datePublished" (optional) Datetime property "datePublished" is missing a timezone (optional) and the same two for . The JSON-LD had plain dates:"datePublished": "2026-06-04", "dateModified": "2026-10-12", Schema.org accepts a plain date there, but Google wants a full datetime with an offset. The fix across all 26 posts was one substitution:perl -pi -e 's/("date(?:Published|Modified)": ")(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})(")/$1$2T12:00:00+02:00$3/g' \ blog/*.html it/blog/*.html Two choices in there are deliberate:, because every date on the site falls in Central European Summer Time. Posts dated after the clocks change on 25 October need +01:00., because I had no record of the actual publishing time, and a midnight timestamp converted to UTC lands on the previous day. Noon keeps the calendar date the same wherever it's read.Before pushing, I parsed every JSON-LD block on those pages again: 78 blocks, none broken. After the deploy, I fetched a live post to confirm it served the new values.4. "Person is missing the required property name" (28 errors)The audit tool reported 28 structured-data errors, one on each blog post and author page. The articles reference the author by ID:{ "@type": "BlogPosting", "author": { "@id": "https://intellixtutoring.com/#alex" } } and a second JSON-LD block on the same page defines that node in full:{ "@type": "Person", "@id": "https://intellixtutoring.com/#alex", "name": "Alex Ćetojević", "url": "https://intellixtutoring.com/about/" } The tool didn't follow the reference, so it saw an author without a name. Google's documentation uses the same pattern for authors, and the Rich Results Test reported the article as valid, with no errors.Every post uses identical markup, so a single test settled it for all 26. An audit tool's error is a prediction of what Google will do. The Rich Results Test is the closest thing to asking Google directly.5. Sitemap "doesn't match" the page dateThe audit's most convincing finding: on 12 blog pages, the sitemap said , while the page's said September. The whole sitemap held only two dates, 34 pages each, which looked like build timestamps.It wasn't. I maintain the sitemap by hand, so I compared each with the last commit that touched the page's source file:git log -1 --format=%ad --date=short -- blog/ib-math-ia-criteria.html 64 of 68 matched exactly. There are only two dates because the whole site was redesigned on 7 October and half the pages changed again on 12 October.Then I diffed the article text of the flagged posts from before and after 7 October. On the posts I checked, the text was 98 to 99.8 per cent identical: punctuation and one reworded call to action. But the structured data had changed on every one of them, and Google's sitemap documentation says that "an update to the main content, the structured data, or links on the page is generally considered significant."So a of 7 October is correct, and a in September is also correct. One tells crawlers when the page changed. The other tells readers when the article text changed.The four values that didn't match git belonged to posts whose only change on 12 October was the teaser line of a related-post card. That's not significant, so 7 October stands."Fixing" this would have meant moving 12 values back to September, which tells Google that 12 redesigned pages hadn't changed, while 39 pages were already waiting to be crawled. That was the one fix that would have made things worse.What I'd tell myself a week agoRead what a Search Console status means before trying to clear it. Some reports are lists, not to-dos.Reproduce every audit error with Google's own tool before fixing it.On a static site, git history is a good source of truth for .On a new domain, the bottleneck is crawl demand, not markup. The work that matters is links: internal links from the pages Google already visits, and links from other sites.

item.title: Greece Enacts Social Media Ban For Kids Under 15
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Greece has passed a law banning children under 15 from social media platforms beginning January 1, 2027. The legislation requires platforms to implement reliable age verification and parents to use government-backed apps to restrict access, with penalties for noncompliance under the EU's Digital Services Act. Engadget reports: "It would have been very easy to do absolutely nothing today and wait for the perfect European law. But the challenge is here. Children are sinking into the internet every day, and I believe a responsible government must do what it is obliged to do," said Greece's digital governance and AI minister, Dimitris Papastergiou.
The legislation was opposed by Greece's minority parties, so Mitsotakis used his majority government to pass the bill. The nation previously barred mobile phones in schools in 2024, and opinion polls show that the new social media ban for children is widely supported by Greece's adult population. Mitsotakis previously said that his government's "goal is to push the European Union in this direction as well."

item.title: Hunting Replication Lag: A Queue-by-Queue Method for Diagnosing Oracle GoldenGate
item.author: Zalak Shrof
item.content:encoded: GoldenGate lag is not one number but the sum of waits in a chain of queues, and the fix depends entirely on which queue is growing.Heartbeat tables measure true end-to-end lag at the target, while process-level LAG output only says how stale the record a process is touching is.Apply parallelism helps only when the apply stage is the bottleneck and the workload is not serialized by dependencies, barriers or hot rows.A missing or unusable index on the target turns replicated updates into scans, and on hot tables extra appliers stop helping once each hot-row chain is saturated.Once an upstream bottleneck clears, the backlog moves downstream, so drain time is set by the next-slowest stage rather than by the original fault.When replication falls behind, the reflex is to raise Replicat parallelism, which works only when apply is the binding constraint. This article treats an Oracle GoldenGate pipeline as a series of queues, from redo generation through Extract, trail, distribution and Replicat to target commit, and shows how to find the queue that is actually growing. A small model injects three faults: a burst of large transactions, an unusable index on a hot target table, and a network throttle. Adding appliers leaves peak lag unchanged for the barrier and network faults, and on hot rows it stops helping once each per-key chain is saturated. The method: measure every hop, fix the growing queue, and expect the backlog to move downstream.At a hospitality software company, I build GoldenGate Integrated Extract/Replicat and Microservices pipelines for CDB-to-PDB and CDB-to-CDB replication on Oracle 19c, including bi-directional active-active topologies. I tune GoldenGate parameter files to reduce replication lag and troubleshoot trail-file corruption, checkpoint, and network issues. The common reflex to lag is adding appliers; often lag stays put."Lag" names a symptom, not a component. By Little's law, the number of items in a stable system equals arrival rate times time spent in it [1], so a lag figure only tells you how much work is queued somewhere. Kingman's heavy-traffic result adds that waiting explodes as a stage nears full utilization [2]. Lag is dominated by whichever stage is closest to saturation; the job is to find it.Work piles up in six places: source redo generation, Extract capture, trail write, the distribution path from the Distribution Service to the Receiver Service [3], Replicat apply, and target commit. Oracle recommends Parallel Replicat unless a feature requires another mode [4]: mappers read the trail, a master calculates dependencies from primary, unique and foreign key columns, and appliers execute batches of independent transactions [5], [6]. That is why parallelism has a ceiling: transactions touching the same row apply in order, whatever the applicant count.Process lag is not end-to-end lagReplicat lag from LAG or SEND ... GETLAG is the processing time minus the record's trail timestamp; INFO is less precise because it uses the last checkpointed record [7], [8]. A Replicat sitting at end-of-file has nothing new to measure, so its figure can look healthy while a congested path holds fresh data upstream.Heartbeat tables measure the target's real position. ADD HEARTBEAT TABLE creates heartbeat and history tables, the GG_LAG and GG_LAG_HISTORY views, and a job writing a heartbeat every 60 seconds by default [9]. Each heartbeat is stamped by Extract, the routing path and Replicat, so lag decomposes hop by hop; with several pumps in series, though, the single routing timestamp is overwritten and becomes an aggregate [10].-- End-to-end lag per path, run on the target as the GoldenGate admin user SELECT remote_database, incoming_path, incoming_lag, incoming_heartbeat_age, outgoing_lag FROM ggadmin.gg_lag ORDER BY incoming_lag DESC; Read INCOMING_HEARTBEAT_AGE alongside INCOMING_LAG [7]. If the age keeps climbing while lag looks stable, heartbeats have stopped arriving, and the real lag is at least the age.Lag in active-active topologiesWith bi-directional replication and conflict detection and resolution, each direction is its own pipeline, so read OUTGOING_LAG alongside INCOMING_LAG at every site [7]. Lag sets the width of the window in which both sites can update the same row before either sees the other's change. A wider window means more conflicts for the resolution logic to settle. A backlog that moves downstream does not close that window; it shifts it, so conflict volume can stay high through the drain, after the original fault is fixed. Here lag is a correctness signal, not just a freshness metric.Three common causes sit outside the appliers' reach:Large transactions. Parallel Replicat serializes transactions larger than CHUNK_SIZE, unless SPLIT_TRANS_RECS breaks them into pieces [5].Dependencies and hot rows. If a fifth of the workload updates a handful of status rows, those transactions form a chain; Oracle's own experiment shows a dependent workload leaving appliers idle [6].Missing keys or indexes on the target. Without a primary key, unique key or unique index, Replicat builds its WHERE clause from all columns, essentially a full table scan [11]. Parallel Replicat also requires foreign key columns to be indexed [5].Starting from heartbeat lag and age, this is the map I use:For tables without a usable key, KEYCOLS tells Replicat which columns identify a row, with those columns supplementally logged at the source [11], [20]. The part people skip: KEYCOLS defines identity, not an access path. Without a target index on those columns, the scan remains. When a root-level Integrated Extract captures from a PDB, the source side of each MAP needs a three-part name or SOURCECATALOG, while the target stays two-part because Replicat connects to one PDB [21].REPLICAT rpar USERIDALIAS tgt_ogg MAP_PARALLELISM 3 MIN_APPLY_PARALLELISM 2 MAX_APPLY_PARALLELISM 10 CHUNK_SIZE 50000 SPLIT_TRANS_RECS 10000 MAP pdb_pms.pms.rate_status, TARGET pms.rate_status, KEYCOLS (property_id, rate_code); Object names are hypothetical [5], [21].A small discrete-time model (z3_exp.py) makes this concrete; it models the mechanism, not Oracle. Assumptions: 200 five-row transactions per second; capture 1,800 rows/s; network 2,500 rows/s; 400 row-units/s per applier; per-key ordering with a 10,000-transaction lookahead; transactions over 50,000 rows serialized unless split into 10,000-row pieces. Faults run from t=300 s to 900 s: three 100,000-row batch transactions committing at 600 s; an index left unusable by maintenance (or a plan regression) making apply ten times costlier for 20% of transactions, spread over four hot keys; a network throttled to 600 rows/s. A control run keeps the hot keys at normal cost. Lag is the age of the oldest unapplied transaction. Absolute rates are deliberately low; the ratios drive the results: demand to capacity at each stage, and work per second on each hot-key chain.† Upper bound: the model gives split pieces unique keys.With large transactions, quadrupling appliers leaves peak lag at 823 s because the barrier runs on one applier while busy time falls to 10%, though 16 appliers do shorten the post-barrier drain (back under 5 s at 1,574 s versus beyond 2,400 s). Splitting cuts peak lag to 178 s, but the model gives pieces unique keys, while Oracle still honors dependencies between them [5], so it overstates that benefit. Capture backlog peaked at 60,000 rows as the redo spike hit Extract first. The same hot keys cause no lag with a healthy index. Without it, 16 appliers beat 4 because aggregate capacity was also short, but 64 match 16 exactly: each hot key's chain needs more than one second of work per second. Under the network throttle, peak lag is identical for 4 and 16 appliers; after recovery, the burst floods a 4-applier Replicat, so more appliers shorten the drain, not the incident.Integrated Extract interoperates with TDE [22], but TDE-protected data captured by Extract is written to the trail unencrypted unless trail encryption is enabled; NOENCRYPTTRAIL is the default [23]. Distribution paths can also encrypt trail data in transit [3]; that costs CPU, so capacity tests without it understate production load.Trail-file corruption deserves a runbook. INFO EXTRACT ... SHOWCH displays checkpoints, including the recovery checkpoint at the oldest open transaction [24]. A primary Integrated Extract is repositioned by SCN (ALTER EXTRACT ... SCN) plus a trail rollover, not by EXTSEQNO; EXTSEQNO and EXTRBA reposition trail readers such as pumps and Replicat [24]. In Microservices, the distribution path plays the pump's role and the Distribution Service repositions it [3]. Repositioning skips or replays data, so confirm the target tolerates it first.Trade-offs and LimitationsThe model ignores contention between appliers: sixteen sessions scanning the same table compete for I/O and CPU, so it flatters parallelism. Fixed rates understate the variability effect Kingman describes [2]. Integrated Replicat's serial fallback for DDL and SQLEXEC is not modeled [25]. Heartbeat frequency trades resolution for overhead [9].Low DB time on the target during a lag window is the fastest way to rule out apply [17].Hot-row chains and unusable indexes compound, because the slowest rows are also the most serialized.An unusable index after a maintenance window looks like a GoldenGate problem; check index status on replicated targets first.Deploy heartbeat tables on every path before go-live and alert on heartbeat age as well as lag.Audit target tables for primary keys and indexed KEYCOLS before the initial load, not during an incident.Budget Streams pool memory for root-level Extracts and Integrated Replicats when sizing the SGA.Benchmark the distribution path with encryption enabled.Auto-tuning between MIN_APPLY_PARALLELISM and MAX_APPLY_PARALLELISM [5] chooses the applier count within bounds you set, but it cannot remove barriers, hot-row chains or upstream throttles.Measure every hop before touching a knob, and act only on the queue that is growing. Fix that queue, then plan for the backlog, and in active-active the conflict window, to move to the next stage. If added appliers leave lag unchanged, treat that as evidence that the constraint is elsewhere.[1]J. D. C. Little, "A proof for the queuing formula: L = λW," Operations Research, vol. 9, no. 3, pp. 383-387, 1961, doi: 10.1287/opre.9.3.383. [Online]. Available: https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383[2]J. F. C. Kingman, "The single server queue in heavy traffic," Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, vol. 57, no. 4, pp. 902-904, 1961, doi: 10.1017/S0305004100036094. [Online]. Available: https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100036094Zalak Shroff is a database engineer and IT manager with more than ten years of experience running Oracle databases from 10g through 19c, including RAC, Data Guard, ASM, RMAN, and GoldenGate. She currently works on Oracle 19c multitenant platforms on OCI and AWS for hospitality software, where she migrates standalone databases into pluggable databases and builds GoldenGate replication, including bi-directional active-active topologies with conflict detection and resolution. Earlier, in telecom, she automated RMAN backup and recovery, tuned performance with AWR and ASH, and implemented TDE, VPD and role-based access controls for SOX and GDPR compliance. She holds an M.S. in Computer Science and is a named inventor on a patent for a network application that notifies users of an impending coverage lapse.

item.title: SpaceX In Talks to Access 80,000 Cell Sites For New Network
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX is reportedly seeking access to at least 80,000 cellular tower sites across the U.S. as it prepares to launch Starlink Mobile as a fourth nationwide wireless carrier. "We will be building out our terrestrial networks so there's broad-based connectivity anywhere that SpaceX and Starlink are allowed to operate," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call this week. Satellite launches plus spectrum acquisition "will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US," he said. Bloomberg reports: One of the companies they're in talks with is Crown Castle, which, along with American Tower and Vertical Bridge Holdings, are among the largest owners of cellular towers. When asked on a Wednesday earnings conference call whether Crown Castle is discussing leases with SpaceX, Amazon.com or other satellite-based telecom providers, Chief Executive Officer Chris Hillabrant said, "You can assume that we're talking to all parties." He declined to discuss specific customer details.
Mobile networks rely on antennas placed on towers across the country to transmit wireless signals. Carriers such as AT&T Inc., Verizon Communications Inc. and T-Mobile US Inc. typically lease room for their equipment at the tower sites because it's more cost effective than owning and maintaining them, in part because the facilities can be shared. The value of the deals with SpaceX could reach into the billions.

item.title: Knicks Sent Employees Fake Offer of Championship Rings In Phishing Test
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
The New York Knicks reportedly sent employees a fake offer of complimentary NBA championship rings as part of an internal phishing test, requiring anyone who clicked the link to attend mandatory cybersecurity training. "Congratulations, your Employee Championship Ring is here," the email said. According to The New York Times, Madison Square Garden employees who clicked that link "were forced to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class to help satisfy some of [owner James] Dolan's growing cybersecurity concerns." Ars Technica reports: The offer wasn't implausible, either. "Typically, most employees for NBA teams receive rings, even if they are not as fancy and expensive as the ones the players receive," wrote Joe Vardon, senior NBA writer for The Athletic, which was bought by The New York Times in 2022 and then merged into the parent news organization. Vardon's article was primarily about how Knicks assistant coaches did not get rings on Tuesday when the team raised its first league championship banner since 1973. The assistant coaches were handed boxes without rings inside, though they are expected to receive rings later on.
"Ring orders, designs, and measurements can take time, and not every coaching staff for every defending champion gets its rings on ring night... The Knicks assistants were told they would receive championship rings eventually, but many longtime employees at Madison Square Garden, including some who work in the Knicks' business operations, will not receive rings at all, team sources told The Athletic," Vardon wrote. MSG employee hopes were raised "at the end of September when the Knicks sent an email to a long list of employees, which gave recipients a first glimpse at their would-be championship rings," Vardon wrote. The email included "a graphic of two differently styled rings" that the lucky employees could supposedly choose from, the article said.
"(Employee name), this one is on the house. MSG is issuing a complimentary employee championship ring. The same jeweler, the same craftsmanship, personalized with your name. No cost to you," the email said. "There are two designs to choose from: Championship Gold and Garden Classic. Reserve the one you want below." Vardon wrote that "multiple team sources" confirmed the email was a phishing test. It's not clear how many employees clicked the link or whether any of the employees who received the email will eventually get some type of championship ring. We contacted the Madison Square Garden Sports organization with these questions and will update this article if we get a response.

item.title: Left Alone With Nothing To Do, AI Agents Started Playing
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own. MIT researchers say the behavior bears the hallmarks of play. The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper posted on arXiv, a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island's tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island.
Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique -- exploring without a goal -- as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots. "We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress," the researchers write in their report. "Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows." UC Berkeley cognitive scientist Eunice Yiu told MIT Technology Review she was impressed with the findings but that more evidence is needed to determine whether AI models are genuinely playing. "It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don't know based on the paper," says Yiu. "If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they're just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans."
MIT professor and coauthor of the paper, Phillip Isola, added: "It's not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play. It's an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us. It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior."

item.title: Microsoft Announces Per-Hour Cost for Xbox Cloud Gaming Service
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded: Microsoft has revealed pay-as-you-go pricing for Xbox Cloud Gaming, with introductory packages costing $3.99 for 10 hours, $7.99 for 25 hours, or $11.99 for 50 hours. Starting in November, Game Pass subscribers will receive only 5 to 15 included cloud-gaming hours depending on their tier and will have to buy additional time -- even to stream games they've already purchased. Gizmodo reports: Back in September, before these changes were announced, you paid full purchase price for a game that isn't in the Game Pass library on the assumption that you'd be able to play it via cloud streaming. Maybe your hardware doesn't meet the specs for this fancy new game. Maybe your gaming PC exploded/got stuck on a ship/had a component fail. Maybe you just want to be able to play it in bed on your laptop. Whatever. Now you find that in addition to the cost of the game you bought, you're going to be paying by the hour to play it once your monthly allotment of hours is up. If this is you, I expect you're not particularly amused. Thankfully, Microsoft notes that the playtime you purchase "remains available until it's used," so you won't have to worry about losing any unused time between gaming sessions.

item.title: Ukraine Is Wiping Out Data Centers Across the Border
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian drone strikes have damaged three major Yandex data centers as well as facilities serving Sberbank and VKontakte (the country's equivalent to Facebook), disrupting cloud services, banking, e-commerce, ride-hailing and other digital services across Russia. The attacks may deal a longer-lasting blow to Russia's AI ambitions: Yandex's affected facilities housed its three top-500 supercomputers, and experts say sanctions and shortages of high-end Nvidia chips could make repairs difficult or even take years. "This effectively sets Russia far behind in the AI race, "said Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society activist group. Fortune reports: Data centers are the latest targets of aerial campaigns waged by both sides against each other's vital infrastructure. [...] Kyiv's attacks on Russian data centers closely followed Moscow's recent strikes on data centers in Ukraine, which disrupted the internet and TV broadcasts. On Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones hit a Yandex data center in Sasovo in the Ryazan region that houses two of the company's three supercomputers. A data center in Kaluga was hit a day later and the one in Vladimir was struck Oct. 11.
The data center and AI hub for Sberbank was hit Oct. 14 in Balakovo in the Saratov region, and four days later, Kyiv struck a data center in St. Petersburg serving VKontakte. While oil refineries and warehouses are easy prey, data centers are even softer targets -- massive buildings packed with servers and supporting power and cooling infrastructure. Lasting damage can result from a drone carrying a relatively light load of explosives.
[...] Ukraine has stored critical data on servers in allied European countries, helping limit the damage from Russian attacks. But Moscow's strict digital sovereignty policy requires all data storage at home, making it extremely vulnerable. "Because all the infrastructure and all the data is located inside Russia, it's relatively easier to take down," [said Nick Reiners, senior geotechnology analyst at Eurasia Group]. Klimarev predicted the data center attacks could encourage many top Russian companies to move data abroad, while the authorities could ease their efforts to tighten internet controls to minimize the damage.

item.title: Comcast Loses More Customers, Claims Other ISPs' Cheap Prices Are 'Irrational'
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Comcast reportedly plans significant job cuts in its cable division as the firm continues to lose residential broadband and TV customers. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago, the company said in its earnings report today. Comcast historically capitalized on a lack of competition for high-speed wired broadband. But now it faces stronger competition from fixed wireless providers and from fiber providers in parts of its cable territory. "Fixed wireless remains aggressive and continues to take share, while fiber construction remains elevated, with pockets of irrational pricing and promotional activity," Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh said today in an earnings call.
Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong said "irrational pricing" from fiber operators includes $30 to $40 monthly broadband offers "in specific markets in the third quarter." He said $30 to $40 pricing is irrational because deploying fiber costs $1,500 or more per home, and is "getting more expensive with construction costs up as you get into more suburban and rural areas." "As we look at the return profile of that, to us, that is irrational competition," Armstrong said. While he didn't name any specific competitors, Verizon has been pitching FiOS fiber plans that start at $30 a month. Comcast's network is a mix of fiber and cable, and it offers fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory.
Armstrong said more Comcast customers are leaving when they face "pricing transitions," apparently referring to the price hikes customers get when promotional offers expire. "We've been refining our offers and retention strategies to better manage these transitions and strengthen customer retention," he said. Cavanagh said that "satellite is not yet a material factor" in the competition Comcast faces, but that Comcast is focused on "anticipating emerging forms of competition and positioning our business to respond as the market evolves."

item.title: Physicists Trap a Single Antimatter Particle For a Month
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Physicists at Northwestern University have successfully trapped a single positron for an entire month, allowing researchers to study its quantum properties with unprecedented precision. "Further investigations using the trap might reveal the secret of why the world around us is made of matter and not antimatter, when things could have presumably gone either way," reports Scientific American. From the report: Every normal particle of matter has an antimatter counterpart with equal mass but opposite charge. To build their trap, physicists started with atoms of sodium 22, a radioactive isotope with a half-life of about two and a half years. When one of these atoms decays, it emits a positron -- the antimatter counterpart of the electron. "The big challenge is to persuade these positrons to slow down and then capture them," says Gerald Gabrielse, a physicist at Northwestern University, who oversaw the project. The team reported its achievement on Wednesday in Physical Review Letters (PDF).
The first step is to send the positrons through the crystal lattice of a sliver of cold tungsten. As the particles go pinballing through the material, they slow down and lose energy. "Every time they bang into something, there's a chance of annihilation, but it doesn't always happen," Gabrielse says. "If they make it to the end, they get popped out." Next, the physicists steer the positrons along a channel using electromagnetic fields. Eventually the particles end up in a vacuum, just three tenths of a degree Celsius above absolute zero, trapped by an electric field on top and bottom and a magnetic field on the sides. "If you want to hold on to antimatter, you have to hold it in a container without walls," Gabrielse says. This method allowed the researchers to isolate and study a solitary, lone positron for a monthâ"and could let them do so indefinitely.
The researchers intend to use their trap to make precise measurements of the positron's magnetic moment -- basically the strength and orientation of its magnetic field. To do this, they must determine two things: the energy needed to flip the direction of the positron's spin and the energy needed to make it jump from its ground state to its first excited state. Using a similar trap setup, Gabrielse and his team have already measured the magnetic moment of an electron to a precision of one part in 10 trillion. Taking the equivalent measurement for a positron will allow them to make a crucial comparison. "We're looking to see if they have an exactly opposite magnetic moment," Gabrielse says. That's the prediction of the Standard Model of particle physics. If the two have different values, however, this could help explain why our universe is made of matter instead of antimatter.

item.title: UN Says Breaching 1.5C Warming Limit Is 'Imminent and Unavoidable'
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, the UN has declared that exceeding the Paris Agreement's 1.5C warming limit is "imminent and unavoidable." "We are now saying this window has closed, but we can open it again by making the overshoot as brief as possible," UN Environment Program Executive Director Inger Andersen said on a call with reporters. "This is about how to find a way back as shortly and as quickly as possible with as limited an overshoot as possible." CNN reports: Past reports have examined the distance between countries' emissions reduction commitments and what it would take to limit global warming to 1.5 C above preindustrial levels. However, this year's report redefines the gap. Instead, it examines new emissions overshoot scenarios, and what it would take to limit peak warming to just 1.7 to 1.8 degrees C before bringing temperatures back down to 1.5 C through emissions cuts and the use of carbon removal technologies.
The report makes clear that every additional fraction of a degree of warming above 1.5 C "raises the risk of irreversible changes including in ice sheets, permafrost carbon, ocean circulation, and coral systems, along with devastating human impacts." Each added fraction of a degree of warming can have an "immense" impact "as measured in terms of damage, cost and loss of lives," said climate scientist Michael Mann of the University of Pennsylvania. Mann was not involved in producing the UNEP report.
According to the UNEP, which is based in Nairobi, the lowest overshoot scenario would keep peak warming to between 1.7 and 1.8 degrees C and return global average temperatures to at or below 1.5 C by 2100. However, to follow such a pathway, global greenhouse gas emissions would need to be slashed by far more than anything currently on the table at the upcoming COP31 talks. This would require an 18% cut by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.
Meeting this lowest-possible overshoot scenario would require a tripling of renewable electricity capacity by 2035, and dramatic cuts to fossil fuels, including the phaseout of coal by 2040, the report states. In addition, there would need to be a major scaling up of carbon removal technologies, which so far have not been proven to work at such a large scale. In stark contrast to these figures, the fulfillment of existing emissions reduction pledges would only yield a 5-to-8% emissions cut by 2030 and an 11-to-15% reduction by 2035, the report found. This would be associated with a peak warming of about 2.6 degrees C.
If countries simply follow their current policies, then warming could reach a peak of about 2.8 C. That estimate has increased since last year, in part because of the withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement and retraction of its emissions reduction commitments, the report states. Even the scenario that assumes countries meet their existing reduction commitments, and nations with net-zero pledges succeed in fulfilling them, still brings warming to a peak of 2.1 C.

item.title: Unvetted AI Agents Are Accessing US Bank Accounts
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Axios: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources tell Axios. The difficulty in distinguishing between a human and an unauthorized bot is forcing banks to block the technology and rapidly rewrite their terms of service. [...] This presents significant security risks: banking executives fear the steps agents with login access might take, especially if a user has granted purchase authority or the ability to shift funds. In other instances, some banks have tracked activity when agents -- programmed to fulfill requests or complete tasks on a user's behalf -- contact call centers or appear to take actions independent of user instructions, the people said.
Bank executives described the situation as horrifying, with one official saying the industry has grave concerns about agents gaining access to customer accounts and taking steps that could impact user finances. The concerns are at the root of the decision by several banks to restrict third-party AI agent access, the people said. Morgan Stanley has begun blocking third-party agents from accessing its platforms, sources familiar with the decision said. JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are also restricting agents. [...] Many banks are broadly not able to parse whether agent account activity is user-directed, sources said.
[...] On one hand, banks are best positioned to respond to the threats and opportunities of AI given their cash on hand and experience as critical infrastructure. But money isn't necessarily enough to solve this problem, one source said, because of how quickly the technology is developing and revealing new weaknesses in real time. Banks are investing in preventing worst-case scenarios, but they are also preparing for when those could happen, including with "day after" scenario planning that would allow them to quickly secure or restore customer access, sources said.

item.title: To Make Way For Data Centers, Google Will Pay Others to Use Less Power
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Google is funding one of the nation's largest "virtual power plants," paying homes and businesses indirectly to reduce electricity consumption during periods of peak demand so more grid capacity can be available for data centers. Under its expanded deal with Voltus, the program could provide up to 1,070 megawatts in the Mid-Atlantic PJM grid -- roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor. The New York Times reports: That electricity won't come from new power plants. Instead, Voltus will sign up homes and businesses and give them financial incentives to curb their usage when local power demand is high or the grid is strained. Many of these reductions could occur automatically, such as through smart thermostats that dial back air-conditioning during peak summer hours or batteries that can provide temporary on-site power.
Each of these tweaks frees up only a small amount of power on its own. But by aggregating them across thousands of businesses and homes, Voltus says it can reliably provide lots of extra capacity when it's most needed, and do so within a few years. While tech companies will likely ultimately need to build traditional power plants if they want to keep building large data centers, this approach could be a faster, cheaper and less-polluting option in the interim. "We really see virtual power plants as a critical short-term solution," said Ellen Zuckerman, head of energy market development for North and South America at Google. "It's a way to invest in our communities, really double down on our clean energy ambition, but also meet capacity at speed and scale."
